author_response_spans.text: ## **Response to Reviewers**

||**Response to Reviewers**| |---|---| |**Manuscript #**|NCOMMS-24-00588-T| |**Title**|RPA transforms RNase H1 to a bidirectional exoribonuclease for
processive RNA–DNA hybrid cleavage| |**Corresponding**
**Authors**|Bo Sun (ShanghaiTech University) & Wei Li (Guangzhou Medical
University)| |**Contributing**
**Authors**|Yanan Li, Chao Liu, Xinshuo Jia, Lulu Bi, Zhiyun Ren, Yilin Zhao, Xia
Zhang, Lijuan Guo, YanlingBao, & CongLiu,|

We greatly appreciate the comments and suggestions from the reviewers to improve our manuscript. We have carefully considered each comment and taken comprehensive actions as detailed in the following response. The changes made to the manuscript are highlighted in red. We begin below with a summary of major changes in the main text. This is followed by a detailed, point-by-point response to each comment. Each comment is shown in black (bold) and is followed by our response in blue (not bold).
## **Summary of major changes to the manuscript:**

1. In addition to 5 nM and 50 nM RNase H1, we performed the single-molecule optical tweezers assay under 10 nM and 15 nM RNase H1 and monitored that the increase in hybrid length was in company with a few RNase H1 proteins moving in the same direction along the hybrid. This finding supports that RNase H1 first acted as an endonuclease, nicking the RNA in the hybrid, followed by the directional RNA degradation as an exonuclease. We also demonstrated the binding preference of RNase H1 for nicked hybrid. These data have been updated in the new **Supplementary Figs. 5** and **6** .

2. We carried out additional smFRET experiments with an RNase H1 mutant and the results further strengthen the conclusion that the hybrid duplex is unwound by RNase H1 prior to the excision. These data have been updated in the new **Supplementary Figs. 13** and **14** .

3. We conducted a series of experiments with differently labelled hybrid substrates and confirmed that the unwinding step of RNase H1 is indeed 6 bp. These data have been updated in the new **Supplementary Figs. 15, 16** and **17** .

4. In the optical tweezers assay, we simultaneously monitored RNase H1 and RPA during the hybrid degradation process and found that a single RNase H1 protein maintained the location at the active ss-ds hybrid junctions in both directional and bidirectional RNA degradation events. These results confirmed the RNase H1’s 5′-to-
_Page R1_
3′ and 3’-to-5’ exoribonuclease activities and have been updated in the new **Supplementary Figs. 21** .

5. We examined the unidirectional RNA degradation events of RNase H1 in the presence of RPA and found that they all proceeded in a 3’-5’ directionality. These data have been updated in the new **Supplementary Fig. 20** .
**Response:** we thank the reviewer for his/her positive remarks and critical criticisms, which are highly valuable for us to improve the manuscript.
## **Critical comments:**
## **1. Without evoking an exonuclease/unwinding activity, the processive activity could**

**be interpreted by endonucleolytic cleavage every few bp by a single enzyme followed by spontaneous release of the short RNA. This would still be consistent with the observed dependence of the cleavage rate on GC content. This possibility should be ruled out or discussed.**

**Response:** we thank the reviewer for providing an alternative explanation for the observed processive hybrid cleavage by RNase H1. The exonuclease activity of RNase H1 was further supported by the additional assays allowing for the simultaneous monitoring of both RPA and RNase H1. We refer the reviewer to our response to the second comment raised by the reviewer for more details.

To examine whether the hybrid unwinding occurred prior to the RNA excision, we reexamined our data and carried out additional experiments. In addition to the GCdependence, three datasets further strengthen the conclusion:
First, after re-examining out smFRET data, quick high-to-low FRET bursts were spotted in the real-time traces during the degradation of 3'-RDH, GC-RDH, and AU-RDH by
_Page R2_
RNase H1. Given that the hybrid unwinding is reversible and yet the nucleotide excision is not, these transitions reflect the hybrid rewinding events ( **Figs. R1, 2d and 2g** ).
**==> picture [417 x 116] intentionally omitted <==**
_**Fig. R1 (new Supplementary Fig. 13).** Representative traces show RNase H1 degrading 3’-RDH (_ _**a** ), GC-RDH (_ _**b** ) and AU-RDH (_ _**c** ) with rewinding._

Second, to directly examine unwinding activity of RNase H1, we carried out the smFRET experiment with a nuclease-deficient RNase H1 mutant, RNase H1-D264N ( **Fig. R1a** ). RNase H1-D264N acted on the 3'-RDH substrate with abrupt bursts in 31% of the 367 trajectories, and the _E_ of this state was consistent with the initial burst of RNase H1 activity ( **Fig. R1b** ), in favor of the hybrid unwinding activity of RNase H1.
**==> picture [385 x 156] intentionally omitted <==**

_**Fig. R2 (new Supplementary Fig. 14). a.** A representative gel showing the nuclease activity of RNase H1-D264N (15 nM) on the FAM-labeled RDH substrate._ _**b.** A representative smFRET trajectory showing RNase H1-D264N processing 3’-RDH in real time. The red arrows highlight the unwinding signal._

Third, the 6-bp step size monitored in the smFRET assay is inconsistent with 3-nt cleavage products. if spontaneous RNA release were the case, the step size would be expected to be the same as that of the cleavage products.
Taken together, the continuous degradation of RNA in RNA-DNA hybrids by RNase H1 involves unwinding activity. We have updated statement of the results on **Page 12** in our new manuscript.
_Page R3_

_“Given that the nucleotide excision is an irreversible process, the notion that RNase H1 unwinds the hybrid prior to cleavage is further substantiated by the transient backward stepping in the process of RNase H1 degrading all three substrates - (Supplementary Fig. 13) and the sudden FRET bursts monitored when RNase H1 D264N, a nuclease-deficient mutant (_ _**Ref. R1** ), acted on the 3'-RDH substrate (Supplementary Fig. 14).”_
_**Reference**_
_R1. Nguyen HD, Yadav T, Giri S, Saez B, Graubert TA, Zou L. Functions of Replication Protein A as a Sensor of R Loops and a Regulator of RNaseH1. Mol Cell 65, 832-847 (2017)._

## **2. Without evoking a new 5'-to-3' exonuclease activity, the bidirectional degradation results could be interpreted by RNase H1 making an endonuclease cut near the junction, translocating 3' to 5' to release the short fragment, and doing so repeatedly. One way to test this is to use labeled RNase H1 and track their localization at the ssds boundaries marked by labeled RPA or RNA.**

**Response:** we thank the reviewer for this comment and suggestion. Following that, we utilized Cy3-labeled RNase H1 (RNase H1-Cy3) and eGFP-fused RPA (RPA-eGFP) to monitor the process of RNA degradation. In the cases of both unidirectional and bidirectional RNA degradation, a single RNase H1 was consistently recorded at the growing edges of the ssDNA-coated RPA, indicating RNase H1 locating at the active ssds hybrid junctions. Along with the expansion of RPA along the ssDNA, the RNase H1 proteins maintained the location at the RPA edges ( **Fig. R3a** ). Furthermore, under these conditions, the typical waiting time before a single RNase H1 protein associated with the hybrid was found to be in the range of tens of seconds ( **Supplementary Fig. 4a** ), ruling out the possibility of repeated association and dissociation of RNase H1. Therefore, bidirectional RNA degradation is indeed a result of both 5'-to-3' and 3'-to5' exonuclease activities of RNase H1. These datasets have updated in the new **Supplementary Figs. 4 and 21** .
**==> picture [299 x 172] intentionally omitted <==**
_**Fig. R3 (new Supplementary Fig. 21). a** and_ _**b** . Representative kymographs show RNase H1-Cy3 degrading RNA in RNA–DNA hybrid in presence of RPA-eGFP_
_Page R4_

_unidirectionally (_ _**a** ) and bidrectionally (_ _**b** ). The corresponding length of the examined molecule is shown below the kymographs. The experiment was carried out in a channel containing 5 nM RNase H1-Cy3 (green) and 5 nM hRPA-eGFP (purple) under 10 pN._

## **3. The authors suggest that RNase H1 can operate as a molecular motor. However, it doesn't contain a typical ATPase domain. What is the energy source that drives its directional movement? Is it the entropy gain from RNA release? This should be discussed.**

**Response:** we are grateful for the reviewer’s comment. The cyclic coupling between duplex unwinding and nucleotide excision may potentially be elucidated by a springloaded mechanism, which is previously proposed for several nucleases. The chemical energy released from the hydrolysis of the nucleic acid chain is converted into elastic energy, enabling the unwinding of several base pairs in bursts and facilitating directional translocation ( **Ref. R2** ). We have further elaborated on the energy source in our discussion, which can be found on **Page 19** of the manuscript.

“ _This cyclic coupling between duplex unwinding and nucleotide excision could be - explained by a spring loaded mechanism wherein the chemical energy released from the hydrolysis of the nucleic acids chain is converted into elastic energy for unwinding several base pairs in bursts and translocating directionally (_ _**Ref. R2** )._ ”
## _**Reference**_
_R2. Lee G, Bratkowski MA, Ding F, Ke A, Ha T. Elastic coupling between RNA degradation and unwinding by an exoribonuclease. Science_ _**336** , 1726-1729 (2012)._
## **Other comments:**

## **1. It should be made clear that for the most cases in this study (e.g., Fig 2A, 2E, 5A), RNase H1 first needs to make an endonuclease cut before undergoing processive translocation (i.e., exonuclease cleavage). Whether this prerequisite is obligatory should be discussed.**

**Response:** we thank the reviewer for the question and agree with the reviewer that RNase H1 first needs to make an endonuclease cut before the processive RNA degradation. We carried out the optical tweezers assay under 10 and 15 nM RNase H1 and found a few RNase H1 proteins moving along the hybrid in the same direction while the hybrid was digested ( **see our following response** ). Given that it is unlikely to have many preformed nicks in the hybrid, a nick must be generated first by RNase H1 before the exonucleolytic cleavage.

We also constructed the nicked RNA–DNA hybrid ( **Fig. R4a** ) and RNase H1 was spotted at the nick in over 80 % of the examined substrates (n = 25), indicating RNase H1 indeed prefers to bind the nicked hybrid under the lower concentration ( **Fig. R4b** ).
_Page R5_
We have added these datasets in the Supplementary materials and revised the manuscript by stating:

_“It is conceivable that a single RNase H1 enzyme initially functions as endonuclease, creating a nick in the hybrid, following which it transformed to an exonuclease and directionally degraded RNA from the nick. It is also noteworthy that RNase H1 has the binding preference for the nicked hybrid.”_
**==> picture [365 x 325] intentionally omitted <==**

_**Fig. R4 (new Supplementary Fig. 6). a.** Schematic of the construction of a nicked RNA– DNA hybrids template used in the optical tweezers assays._ _**b.** Representative kymographs showing the binding of RNase H1-Cy3 (green) to a nicked RNA–DNA hybrid without degradation in the presence 1 mM Ca[2+] (80%, n = 25). The RNase H1Cy3 protein bound to the nick is indicated by a yellow arrow._

**2. The authors conclude that RNase H1 uses different mechanisms to degrade RNA depending on the enzyme concentration (endo at high concentration vs. exo at low concentration). However, it could simply be because the enzyme has a higher probability of binding and initiating a cut at a higher concentration. Using an intermediate concentration of RNase H1 (between 5 and 50 nM) may help address this issue. On this note, the bulk cleavage experiments were conducted with 10 or 15 nM RNase H1.**
**Response:** we are grateful for the reviewer’s comment. Following that, we conducted
_Page R6_

the optical tweezers assays under 10 and 15 nM RNase H1 ( **Fig. R5** ). The results showed that the directional RNA degrading events on a single substrate increased with the increase in RNase H1 concentration. Importantly, many monitored RNase H1 moved in the same direction, suggestion the directional exonuclease activity. Under a high RNase H1 concentration, it is imaginable that the adequate coating of RNase H1 along the hybrid would restrict their active movement for the exonucleolytic cleavage, wherein their endonuclease activity plays a dominant role in RNA degradation. We have toned down our statement regarding the dependence of the nucleolytic type of RNase H1 on the protein concentration and incorporated the abovementioned discussion.
**==> picture [417 x 181] intentionally omitted <==**

_**Fig. R5 (new Supplementary Fig. 5). a** and_ _**b** . Representative kymographs showing 12.3-kbp RNA–DNA hybrid was degraded by 10 nM (_ _**a** ) or 15 nM (_ _**b** ) RNase H1-Cy3. The corresponding length of the examined molecule is shown below the kymographs._
## **3. Gel results for the construction of the 7.4-kbp RNA–DNA hybrid should be shown.**

**Response:** we apologize for not providing the gel result regarding the construction of the 7.4-kbp RNA–DNA hybrid in the original manuscript. This result can be found in the new **Supplementary Fig. 1b** . For the RNA–DNA hybrid substrate, we showed the ssRNA, ssDNA, purified ssDNA and dsDNA by agarose gel electrophoresis.
**==> picture [194 x 153] intentionally omitted <==**
_**Fig. R6 (new Supplementary Fig. 1b).** A representative gel shows the ssRNA, ssDNA, purified ssDNA and dsDNA by agarose gel electrophoresis._
_Page R7_
## **4. Is the observed RNase H1 processivity limited by enzyme dissociation or photobleaching? What is the labeling efficiency of RNase H1-Cy3?**

**Response:** the fluorescence signal of RNase H1-Cy3 can typically last for over 120 s before photobleaching in the imaging buffer containing 0.8% D-glucose, 1 mg/ml glucose oxidase, 0.4 mg/ml catalase and 2 mM Trolox, whereas the processivity of RNase H1 is typical around 85 s. Despite these facts, we could not totally eliminate the photobleaching effect. Thus, we revised the manuscript by stating:
_“Please note that the processivity is possibly underestimated due to photobleaching of RNase H1-Cy3…”_
The labeling efficiency of RNase H1 is around 70%, which has now been incorporated into the methods in the revised manuscript.

**5. The fact that human RPA also stimulates scRNase H1 does not exclude the possibility of direct RPA-RNase H1 interaction, given the similarities between the human and yeast proteins. Indeed, Ref 22 reported a direct interaction between hRPA and hRNase H1. Therefore, the effect of RPA on RNase H1's degradation activity may not be solely due to enhanced hybrid unwinding.**
**Response:** we are grateful for the reviewer’s comment and have discussed the possibility of the interaction of RNase H1 and RPA promoting the activity of RNase H1.

_“The direct interactions of RNase H1 with RPA may also help with its exonuclease activity. RPA has been previously demonstrated to promote the association of RNase H1 to RNA–DNA hybrids. This promotion may help recruit RNase H1 to the hybrid fork and maintain its longstanding association for processive hybrid cleavage”_

## **6. The 6-bp/3-nt unwinding model needs more evidence to substantiate, ideally with substrates of different lengths between the FRET donor and acceptor. Otherwise, the conclusion should be toned down.**

**Response:** we thank the reviewer for the comment. Following the suggestion, we have constructed smFRET experiment with 3’-RDH substrates containing different lengths between the FRET donor and acceptor (12 bp-RDH). By using the 12 bp-RDH, real-time trajectories and the TDP obtained with the substrate consistently displayed two stepwise increments in _E_ ( **Fig. R7a** and **b,** from 0.57 to 0.73, and 0.73 to 0.99), which also predict ~ 6-bp (12/2) duplex unwinding in each cycle. To further identify the 6-bp unwinding model, we prepared a tailed RDH substrate containing a 6-nt ssDNA at the 5′ end (6 bp-RDH) to mimic a hydrolytic intermediate of the 12 bp-RDH substrate. We found that after the RNase H1 binding, the initial _E_ state of 6 bp-RDH substrate (about ~ 0.73) was similar with the first incremental _E_ value. During the process of RNA degradation, one sudden increment in _E_ from 0.73 to 0.99 was monitored with 6 bpRDH substrate, which is coincided with the last step detected with the 12 bp-RDH
_Page R8_

substrate ( **Fig. R7c** and **d** ). The missing step from 0.57 to 0.73 in 6 bp-RDH substrate and the coincidence of the last two _E_ states in 6 bp-RDH and 12 bp-RDH substrate support the cyclic 6-bp hybrid unwinding of RNase H1. This dataset has been updated as new **Supplementary Fig 17** . In the revised manuscript we state that:

_“Consistently, experiments with the 12t-RDH hybrid substrate (12-nt ssDNA at the 5' end) revealed one sudden increment in E from 0.65 to 0.96 (Supplementary Fig. 15c, 15d, Supplementary Table 1). The missing steps and the alignment of the remaining - states support the cyclic 6 base pair hybrid unwinding by RNase H1. We carried out similar smFRET experiments with differently labelled hybrid substrates and ruled out the possibility that the unwinding step depends on the fluorescence labelling (_ _**Supplementary Fig. 17** ).”_
**==> picture [417 x 265] intentionally omitted <==**

_**Fig. R7 (new**_ **Supplementary** _**Fig. 17). a** and_ _**c** . Representative smFRET trajectories show a stepwise increase in E in the process of RNase H1 cleaving the 12 bp-RDH (_ _**a** ) and 6 bp-RDH (_ _**c** ) substrates. The solid purple lines are the fitting results from an automated step-finding algorithm._ _**b** and_ _**d** . The TDPs illustrate FRET transitions in the process of RNase H1 cleaving the 12 bp-RDH (_ _**b** ) and 6 bp-RDH (_ _**d** ) substrates, respectively._

**7. The gel results for bulk cleavage assays need clarification. In Fig 3K, an exonucleolytic mechanism would predict decreasing intensities toward lower bands. But a strong band at 25 nt was observed, indicating a preferred endonucleolytic site. In Fig 5D, why would 5'-to-3' exonucleolytic cleavage of the forked substrate generate a strong band at 16 nt, not 13 nt or other sizes?**
**Response:** we are grateful for the reviewer’s comment. Regarding the strong band at
_Page R9_

25 nt in **Fig. 3k,** there are three cytidylic acids in four nucleotides around 25 nt. It is plausible that the hybrid unwinding is hindered around 25 nt to some extend due to the high GC ratio. As the reviewer pointed out, it might be due to a preferred endonucleolytic site as well.

Regarding the strong band at 16 nt in **Fig. 5D** , it might be a result of the specific forked substrate used. Unlike the blunt-end substrate, the existence of the 10-nt RNA tail might regulate the first cut of RNase H1 from the 5’ end. However, this is only a speculation and we do not have evidence for that.
**Response:** we thank the reviewer for his/her positive remarks and critical criticisms, which are highly important to improve our manuscript and to steer future studies.
## **Major comments:**

**1. The authors claim that RNase H1 acts (on long double-stranded substrates), depending on the concentration, either as endonuclease or as exonuclease. From the obtained results, it seems more plausible that RNase H1 acts first as**
_Page R10_

**endonuclease followed by its processive exonuclease activity. I suspect the KD of RNase H1 binding and cleaving a single site within the long RNA–DNA construct to be in the 10 nM range, effectively making the endonucleolytic pathway irrelevant for the short constructs used in the single-molecule FRET experiments. Thus, for the low concentration (5 nM), only a single binding event followed by processive RNA degradation is observed during the timeframe of the optical tweezers experiment and for the high concentration (50 nM), multiple processive events are initiated simultaneously, leading to a fast degradation of the full RNA, accompanied by a rapid dissociation of all proteins. I suggest that the authors revise their conclusions accordingly. In this context, the formulation “a single” RNase H1 should be revised (page 1 line 28, page 5 line 2).**

**Response:** we are grateful for the reviewer’s comment, which is similar to the second minor comment from Reviewer #1. We completely agree with the reviewer that RNase H1 needs to make an endonuclease cut before exonucleolytic cleavage. We conducted the optical tweezers assays under 10 and 15 nM RNase H1 ( **Fig. R5** ). The results showed that the directional RNA degrading events on a single substrate increased with the increase in RNase H1 concentration. Importantly, many monitored RNase H1 moved in the same direction, suggestion the directional exonuclease activity. Under a high RNase H1 concentration, it is imaginable that the adequate coating of RNase H1 along the hybrid would restrict their active movement for the exonucleolytic cleavage, wherein their endonuclease activity possibly plays a dominant role in RNA degradation. As suggested, we have toned down our statement regarding the dependence of the nucleolytic type of RNase H1 on the protein concentration and incorporated the abovementioned discussion in the revised manuscript.

We also constructed a nicked hybrid DNA and found that RNase H1 indeed has a binding preference for the nicked hybrid _**Fig. R4**_ . This means that RNase H1 may has a priority for cleaving damaged hybrid.

Based on the findings from the photobleaching assay we newly performed ( _**Fig. R8**_ ), there was a single RNase H1 in every single cleavage event. The word “single” indicates the monomeric status of RNase H1 responsible for one cleavage event. We chose not to replace the word and hope the reviewer could understand.

**2. I am also not convinced that the use of the term ‘exonuclease’ is the correct one. The activity on the 5’ RNA end as depicted in Fig. 5A is an endonuclease activity on the RNA molecule rather than an exonuclease activity, though it is happening at the double-strand/single-strand junction. It has been previously shown for E. coli RNaseH that this enzyme has a high affinity for such junctions (Ref. 38 in the present manuscript). Furthermore, it was shown that E. coli RNase H acts as a processive exoribonuclease on the 3′ DNA overhang but as an endonuclease on the 5′ DNA overhang of RNA–DNA hybrids. The authors should better highlight these previous results and compare them with their own findings. In my opinion RNaseH1 is a bona fide endonuclease for the RNA but prefers to bind to dsNA-ssNA junctions. There it unwinds the duplex part slightly and then cleaves the RNA or unwinding is supported by RPA. This predominant endonucleolytic activity could be revealed for the 3’ end using the correspondingly adapted experiment in Fig. 5A. Also investigating the RNA cleavage products in presence of RPA might reveal whether longer RNA fragments are removed upon each cleavage step, since unwinding is supported by RPA. This would again support an endonucleolytic mechanism.**

**Response:** we are grateful for the reviewer’s comment. The definition of exonuclease and endonuclease is that “exonucleases act from a free terminus of DNA or RNA, producing mono- and/or oligonucleotides of regular sizes, whereas endonucleases act anywhere within DNA or RNA, producing oligonucleotides” ( **Ref. R3** ) _._ We attributed RNA degradation monitored to exonuclease activities of RNase H1 for the following reasons: first, both smFRET and optical tweezers assays indicated that RNase H1 preferentially binds to the ends (nicks) of RNA and initiates degrading under the lower concentration of RNase H1 ( **Fig. R4** ). Second, according to the optical tweezers assays, the processivity and directionality of RNase H1 also conform to the characteristic of exonucleases ( **Ref. R4** ). Third, we utilized Cy3-labeled RNase H1 (RNase H1-Cy3) and eGFP-fused RPA (RPA-eGFP) to monitor the process of RNA degradation. In the cases of both unidirectional and bidirectional RNA degradation, a single RNase H1 was consistently recorded at the edges of the ssDNA-coated RPA, indicating RNase H1 locating at the ss-ds hybrid junction. Moreover, along with the expansion of RPA along the ssDNA, the RNase H1 proteins maintained the location at the RPA edges ( **Fig. R3a** ). Fourth, following the reviewer’s suggestion, we investigated the RNA cleavage products in presence of RPA. We repeated the bulk cleavage assays with a 53-bp RNA– DNA hybrid substrate in presence of 50 nM RPA. Within this substrate, the 5′ end of the ssRNA was labelled with FAM for fluorescence detection in the PAGE gels. To distinguish the intermediate cleavage products, we supplied RNase H1 with 0.07 mM Mg[2+] to retard the RNA degradation. Under this condition, the cleavage products also exhibited a 3-nt periodicity ( **Fig. R9** ).

_E. coli_ RNase H is an exoribonuclease on the 3’ DNA overhang RNA–DNA hybrid, and an endoribonuclease on the 5’ DNA overhang or blunt-ended hybrids ( **Ref. R5** ). Because it degrades RNA with a nondirectional and distributive mode of action in its previously known role as a non-sequence-specific endonuclease, undergoing multiple
_Page R13_
binding and dissociation events. As suggested, we have incorporated discussions the similarity and difference between scRNase H1 and _E. coli_ RNase H on **Page 17** in our new manuscript.

_“Interestingly, this distinctive characteristic sets scRNase H1 apart from its E. coli counterpart, RNase HI, which relies on a 5' end DNA overhang for the 5'-to-3' exonuclease activity. Moreover, E. coli RNase HI differs from scRNase H1 in the binding preference for RNA ends with DNA overhangs and yet decreased affinity for blunt ends - or internal regions of RNA DNA hybrids (_ _**Ref. R6** ). This discrepancy is likely due to the marked structural differences between E. coli RNase HI, lacking a hybrid binding domain (HBD), and scRNase H1, which features two HBDs (_ _**Ref. R7** ).”_

## **3. I find the usage of the terms “directional translocation” and “molecular motor” difficult, since RNaseH1 is very different from the NTP consuming molecular steppers on single- and double-stranded nucleic acids, such as helicases. To me RNaseH1 rather uses a burnt bridge mechanism in which it generates a cut near the RNA end and subsequently remains bound at the dsNA-ssNA junction due to its high affinity. This is not a classical translocation where the track remains intact.**

**Response:** we greatly appreciate the reviewer’s critical reading and apologize for misleading terms used in the previous manuscript. We have replaced the “translocation” with “movement”, and “molecular motor” with “motor-like” in the revised manuscript.

**4. The statement on page 8 lines 16-17: “Interestingly, experiments with a nicked hybrid molecule displayed preferential binding of RNase H1 to the nick (Fig. S3).” is not sufficiently supported by experimental data. The trace shows two RNase H molecules binding to the DNA, while there was only a single nick introduced to the construct. The authors should show more representative binding traces that strengthen the statement and/or provide statistics for the binding sites.**

**Response:** we apologize for not being explicit on the data presentation. To strengthen the conclusion, we performed additional experiments and have shown more representative kymographs about RNase H1 binding to nicks in the new **Supplementary Fig. 6** . RNase H1 was found to bind to the nick in over 80 % of the
_Page R15_
examined substrates (n = 25) ( **Fig. R4** ). These results indicated that RNase H1 prefers to bind the preformed nick under the low protein concentration.

**5. I find the evidence for an heteroduplex unwinding with 6-bp steps not very convincing. The FRET efficiency is highly nonlinearly dependent on the distance between the fluorophores. Particularly, it saturates at distances smaller than ~3 nm, where no further increase should be expected. Furthermore, Cy3 and Cy5 are known to exhibit changes of the fluorescent emission upon protein binding due to their cistrans isomerization. In my opinion the authors should tone down their conclusions/statements or present other evidence, such as a heteroduplex unwinding for a RNase-dead mutant and/or a more careful mapping of the FRET changes with unwound distance (not only 6 and 17 bp).**

**Response:** we thank the reviewer for raising the essential question regarding whether step size of duplex unwinding is 6 bp in the cleavage process of RNase H1. To address that, we conducted additional experiments with different RDH substrates and RNase H1 mutant.

## RPA transforms RNase H1 to a bidirectional – exoribonuclease for processive RNA DNA hybrid cleavage 

Received: 4 January 2024 Accepted: 21 August 2024 Check for updates 

Yanan Li[1,6] , Chao Liu[2,3,6] , Xinshuo Jia[1] , Lulu Bi[1] , Zhiyun Ren[1,4] , Yilin Zhao[1] , Xia Zhang[1] , Lijuan Guo[1] , Yanling Bao[1] , Cong Liu 5, Wei Li 2,3,4 & Bo Sun 1 

RNase H1 has been acknowledged as an endoribonuclease specializing in the – internal degradation of the RNA moiety within RNA DNA hybrids, and its ribonuclease activity is indispensable in multifaceted aspects of nucleic acid metabolism. However, the molecular mechanism underlying RNase H1mediated hybrid cleavage remains inadequately elucidated. Herein, using single-molecule approaches, we probe the dynamics of the hybrid cleavage by Saccharomyces cerevisiae RNase H1. Remarkably, a single RNase H1 enzyme displays 3′-to-5′ exoribonuclease activity. The directional RNA degradation proceeds processively and yet discretely, wherein unwinding approximately 6-bp hybrids as a prerequisite for two consecutive 3-nt RNA excisions limits the overall rate within each catalytic cycle. Moreover, Replication Protein A (RPA) reinforces RNase H1’s 3′-to-5′ nucleolytic rate and processivity and stimulates its 5′-to-3′ exoribonuclease activity. This stimulation is primarily realized through the pre-separation of the hybrids and consequently transfers RNase - H1 to a bidirectional exoribonuclease, further potentiating its cleavage effi ciency. These findings unveil unprecedented characteristics of an RNase and provide a dynamic view of RPA-enhanced processive hybrid cleavage by RNase H1.

Nucleases are a family of phosphodiesterases tasked with catalyzing the cleavage of the phosphodiester bonds that link nucleotides within nucleic acids[1] . Based on the cleavage mode, nucleases can be classified into endonucleases and exonucleases. The main distinction lies in that endonucleases internally introduce cleavage sites along nucleic acids, whereas exonucleases continuously digest nucleic acids from their ends, producing mononucleotides or oligonucleotides as products[1][,][2] . RNase H are a class of evolutionarily conserved nucleases that appear ubiquitous in bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes[3][,][4] . Since their discovery, RNase H have been widely recognized as endoribonucleases that specifically catalyze the elimination of the RNA moiety of 

RNA–DNA hybrids and R-loops in a sequence non-specific manner[5][,][6] . RNase H are generally involved in the maintenance of genome stability, such as R-loop suppression, DNA replication, homologous recombination (HR)-directed DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair, and ribonucleotide excision repair. Their significance is underscored by the genetic linkage to defective mitochondrial DNA replication and a severe neurological disorder called Aicardi-Goutières syndrome (AGS)[7][,][8] . Among their multifaceted cellular functions, RNase H must deal with hybrids and R-loops with distinct lengths, from single base to several kilobase pairs[9][–][11] . Many vital functions and properties of RNase H have been brought to light in the past few decades[3][,][4][,][7][,][12][,][13] . However,

one intriguing question that remains unanswered is how RNase H at a physiological concentration of a few nanomolar range effectively degrade a long stretch of an RNA–DNA hybrid or an R-loop in cells[14] . 

Based on the sequence similarities and biochemical properties, eukaryotic RNase H are classified into two types (RNase H1 and H2)[3] . While their precise cellular functions may still be under debate, a consensus seems to have emerged that RNase H1 and H2 have overlapping and specialized roles in hydrolyzing illicit hybrids[3][,][4][,][7][,][12][,][13] . In contrast to RNase H2, RNase H1 can work independently of the cell cycle and is more effective in suppressing stable R-loops[15][,][16] . Notably, unlike other RNase H that cleave the hybrids distributively, human RNase H1 is distinct in processing RNA–DNA hybrids processively[17] . Structural and biochemical analysis revealed that the unique N-terminal hybrid binding domain (HBD) of RNase H1 thatis connected to a C-terminal catalytic domain (RNase HC) via a linker of variable length may bestow the processivity[17][,][18] .

This feature holds promise for comprehending RNase H degrading long hybrids and R-loops in vivo. However, the dynamic molecular mechanism underlining RNase H1’s processive cleavage is still lacking. 

It is widely accepted that the nuclease activity of RNase H1 can be regulated by associated proteins[19][–][22] . A key partner of RNase H1 is the single-stranded DNA binding protein, Replication Protein A (RPA), a heterotrimeric protein complex consisting of the RPA70, RPA32, and RPA14 subunits, which also plays a crucial role in DNA replication and recombination[22][–][25] . An in vivo study showed that human RPA colocalizes with both RNase H1 and R-loops in cells, suggesting that these two proteins function together in the R-loop regulation[22] . In addition, biochemical studies have shown that human RPA not only physically interacts with RNase H1 but also stimulates its nuclease activity[22] . Notably, this interaction is specific as it is undetectable between RNase H2 and RPA[22] . Consistently, Escherichia coli single-stranded DNA binding protein (SSB) has also proved to interact with RNase HI, the prokaryotic counterpart of RNase H1, and stimulates its nuclease activity[21][,][22] . Therefore, it seems plausible that RPA coordinates with RNase H1 in processing long hybrids. A thorough understanding of the regulatory role of RPA in RNase H1-mediated hybrid cleavage would advance our knowledge in genome maintenance. 

In this work, we explore the dynamics of Saccharomyces cerevisiae (sc) RNase H1-mediated RNA–DNA hybrid cleavage using singlemolecule approaches. We found that scRNase H1 (hereafter referred to as RNase H1) exhibited concentration-dependent nuclease activities.

A high amount of RNase H1 proteins function mainly as endonucleases that sufficiently bind to a long hybrid and introduce multiple cleavage sites, allowing quick RNA and nuclease dissociation from the DNA. On the other hand, following the RNA nicking, a single RNase H1 nuclease assumes a motor-like role to continuously degrade thousands of base pairs of RNA within a hybrid in the 3′-to-5′ direction before dissociation. In each exonucleolytic cycle, unwinding approximately 6-bp hybrids occurs before two consecutive 3-nt RNA excisions and is the major rate-limiting step. Importantly, besides enhancing the 3′-to5′ hybrid degradation of RNase H1, RPA helps trap thermally frayed ssDNA, allowing RNase H1 to carry out the opposite 5′-to-3′ RNA degradation. The bidirectional exonuclease activity of RNase H1 allows for a processive and fast hybrid degradation. Overall, this work unveils distinctive RNase characteristics and offers insights into the cleavage – of long RNA DNA hybrids and R-loops in cells. 

## Results 

## RNase H1 possesses both endoribonuclease and exoribonuclease activities 

To explore the dynamics of RNase H1-mediated hybrid cleavage, we used dual optical tweezers to monitor the change in the length of a – single RNA DNA hybrid molecule in real time[26] . In this experiment, a 7.4-kbp RNA–DNA hybrid molecule was suspended between one fixed trap and one steered trap via two streptavidin-coated microspheres, 

and a high-frequency feedback system on the steered trap was employed to ensure the force on the hybrid remained constant (Fig, 1a, Supplementary Fig. 1).

Once RNase H1 eliminates the RNA within the suspended hybrid under a constant force, the increase in the molecule length would be expected due to the difference in the elastic response between single-stranded (ss) DNA and double-stranded hybrid (Supplementary Fig. 1c). We started this experiment with 2 nM RNase H1 under a force of 10 pN. As expected, the hybrid length continuously increased at a rate of 3.2 ± 0.1 nm/s (mean ± SEM) (Fig. 1b, c, Supplementary Fig. 2a). Similar results were also obtained under 5 nM RNase H1 with a moderately increased rate of 7.8 ± 0.5 nm/s (mean ± SEM) (Fig. 1b, c, Supplementary Fig. 2b). However, upon elevating the RNase H1 concentration to 50 nM, the molecule length dramatically increased, and the rate is approximately 76-fold (243 ± 11 nm/s, mean ± SEM) faster than that under 2 nM RNase H1 (Fig. 1b, c, Supplementary Fig. 2c). 

The distinct rates detected in the single-molecule assay could be attributable to different types of ribonuclease activities of RNase H1 toward the hybrids. We combined dual optical traps with confocal microscopy to test this hypothesis. Through repeatedly scanning along the suspended hybrid, this combination allowed us to simultaneously record the hybrid length and the fluorescence signals of either the hybrid or RNase H1 during the cleavage (Fig. 1a). Using UTP-Cy3 as one of the nucleotides for RNA synthesis (see Methods), we first constructed a 12.3-kbp fluorescently labelled RNA–DNA hybrid molecule and repeated the optical tweezers assay (Supplementary Fig. 1a). As shown in Fig. 1d and Supplementary Fig. 3a, the transportation of this fluorescently labelled hybrid molecule to a channel containing 50 nM RNase H1 caused an immediate increase in the hybrid length under 10 pN.

At the same time, the fluorescence signal of the RNA disappeared drastically, indicating the dissociation of the RNA from the hybrid. We also conducted experiments using 50 nM Cy3-labelled RNase H1 (RNase H1-Cy3). The association of multiple RNase H1 with the hybrid was immediately noticed in the protein channel. However, this association was followed by a quick disappearance of the fluorescence signal and increased hybrid length within a few seconds (Fig. 1e, Supplementary Fig. 3b). The intense binding of RNase H1 to the hybrid and the quick dissociation of both RNase H1 and RNA support the dominant endonuclease activity that adequately introduces multiple internal cleavage sites within the hybrids, causing the simultaneous dissociation of small RNA fragments and RNase H1 proteins from the hybridized DNA and the drastic increase in the hybrid length. However, in contrast, RNase H1 at 5 nM caused a moderate increase in the length of a fluorescently labelled hybrid (Fig. 1f). Concurrently, a dark region in the middle of the hybrid appeared and subsequently expanded in one direction, suggesting directional RNA degradation (Fig. 1f, Supplementary Fig. 3c). Experiments with RNase H1-Cy3 (5 nM) demonstrated that the increased hybrid length was coupled with the directional movement of the nuclease along the hybrid (Fig. 1g, Supplementary Fig. 3d). Meanwhile, replacing Mg[2+] with Ca[2+] abolished the movement and the increase in the hybrid length (Supplementary Fig. 4a). The photobleaching assay confirmed the monomeric status of the bound RNase H1 proteins (Supplementary Fig. 4b).

Moreover, the waiting time before a single RNase H1-Cy3 protein associating with the hybrid is typically around tens of seconds under this condition, ruling out the possibility that the increase in the hybrid length is a result of multiple RNase H1 proteins (Supplementary Fig. 4a). Based on these findings, the directional RNA degradation observed is attributable to the exonuclease activity of a single RNase H1 protein. Increasing the RNase H1 concentration to 10 nM and 15 nM allowed us to monitor the RNA degradation in company with the simultaneous movements of a few RNase H1-Cy3 proteins in the same direction, further corroborating the exonuclease activity of RNase H1 (Supplementary Fig. 5). These findings also confirmed the 3′-to-5′ cleavage of RNase H1 initiated from the 3′ end of RNA within the hybrids. The increase in E recorded with the 3′-RDH substrate originates from the directional exoribonucleolytic cleavage by RNase H1. The rapid disappearance of the fluorescence signals of the 5′-RDH can be explained by the preferential 3′ RNA binding and nicking of RNase H1 that leads to the detachment of the substrate from the surface. 

## Stepwise RNA cleavage by RNase H1 reveals a dominant ratelimiting step of hybrid unwinding 

Next, we examined the detailed dynamics of RNase H1-mediated 3′RDH cleavage. By carefully analyzing the real-time FRET trajectories, we uncovered a discrete stepwise increase in FRET efficiency, with each increase cycle constituting a burst and a dwell. (Fig. 3a). Taking advantage of an automated step-finding algorithm[30] , we pinpointed four dominant FRET states thatare unevenly distributed in the range of 0.18 to 0.93 (Fig. 3b). A transition density plot (TDP) demonstrated the two-dimensional step for pairs of FRET values before and after each transition[27][,][29][,][30] . This plot presents three stepwise increments in the FRET efficiency between the four states (Fig. 3b). Statistical analysis revealed that the dwell-time histogram follows an exponential decay, supporting a single dominant rate-limiting step during the cleavage (Fig. 3c)[27][,][29][,][31][,][32] . 

Next, we aimed to determine the rate-limiting step in RNase H1mediated exonucleolytic cleavage.

Regarding double-stranded nucleic acids (dsNA) cleavage, exonucleases, such as EXD2 and Rrp44, often involve a major rate-limiting step of dsNA unwinding in their catalytic cycles[27][,][29] . We thus asked whether RNase H1-mediated cleavage necessitates the RNA–DNA hybrid unwinding before nucleotide excision. It is well acknowledged that the ratio of the GC content in the hybrid substrate determines the energy of base stacking and hydrogen bonding[29][,][33][,][34] . If the hybrid unwinding serves as the rate-limiting step, increasing the GC content of the hybrid substrate would prolong the dwell time in its catalytic cycle and reduce the kinetic rate. With this notion in mind, we prepared another RDH substrate and increased the GC content from 50% (3′-RDH) to 88% (GC-RDH) to attenuate the hybrid unwinding, if there is any (Fig. 3d, Supplementary Table 1). Realtime trajectories and the TDP obtained with this GC-RDH substrate 

consistently displayed three stepwise increments in E, resembling the observations with the 3′-RDH substrate (Fig. 3d, e). However, although the dwell-time histogram also showed a single exponential decay, the fitting results yielded a reduced kinetic rate compared to the 3′-RDH substrate (Fig. 3f, j). These findings suggest that the hybrid unwinding is likely a prerequisite for the RNase H1 exonuclease to excise nucleotides and possibly dominates the overall catalytic rate. These conclusions are further sustained by the smFRET experiment with an AU-RDH substrate containing 12% of GC pairs (Fig. 3g, Supplementary Table 1). The introduction of RNase H1 to this substrate led to a similar three-step increase in E (Fig. 3g, h). The dwell-time analysis reveals a kinetic rate twice faster than that of the 3′-RDH substrate (Fig. 3i, j).

Please note that this rate is underestimated as real-time trajectories containing one-step and two-step increments in E from 0.21 to 0.93 were also detectable with the AU-RDH substrate (Supplementary Fig. 12). Given that the nucleotide excision is an irreversible process, the notion that RNase H1 unwinds the hybrid prior to cleavage is further substantiated by the transient backward stepping in the process of RNase H1 degrading all three substrates (Supplementary Fig. 13) and the sudden FRET bursts monitored when RNase H1-D264N, a nucleasedeficient mutant[22] , acted on the 3’-RDH substrate (Supplementary Fig. 14). 

We further asked how many base pairs of the hybrid duplex are unwound and digested in each catalytic cycle. The increase in E from 0.18 to 0.93 corresponds to approximately 17 ribonucleotides digested by RNase H1 (Supplementary Fig. 15), and the three-step increments thus predict ~ 6-bp (17/3) duplex unwinding in each cycle under the assumption that they are equal. To test this hypothesis, we prepared a tailed RDH substrate containing a 6-nt ssDNA at the 5′ end (6t-RDH) to mimic a hydrolytic intermediate of the 3′-RDH substrate (Supplementary Fig. 16a, Supplementary Table 1). The smFRET experiments with this substrate revealed an initial E state of ~0.42 after the binding of RNase H1. In the process of RNA degradation, two sudden increments in E from 0.42 to 0.96 were monitored with this substrate, which coincided with the last two steps detected with the 3′-RDH substrate (Supplementary Fig. 16b). Consistently, experiments with the 12t-RDH hybrid substrate (12-nt ssDNA at the 5′ end) revealed one sudden increment in E from 0.65 to 0.96 (Supplementary Fig. 16c, d, Supplementary Table 1).

The missing steps and the alignment of the remaining states support the cyclic 6-base pair hybrid unwinding by RNase H1. We carried out similar smFRET experiments with differently labelled hybrid substrates and ruled out the possibility that the unwinding step depends on the fluorescence labelling (Supplementary Fig. 17). To further determine the exonucleolytic cleavage products of RNase H1, we performed bulk cleavage assays with a 53-nt RNA–DNA hybrid substrate. Within this substrate, the 5′ end of the ssRNA was labelled with FAM for fluorescence detection in the PAGE gels. To distinguish the intermediate cleavage products, we supplied RNase H1 with 0.07 mM Mg[2+] to retard the RNA degradation. Under this condition, the cleavage products exhibited a 3-nt periodicity (Fig. 3k). In comparison to the 6-bp base pairs involved in each step detected in the smFRET assay (6 bp), the shorter 3-nt nucleolytic products further corroborate that the hybrid unwinding occurs prior to the RNA cleavage for RNase H1. 

Based on these findings, we conclude that scRNase H1 as an exonuclease unwinds 6-bp before two consecutive 3-nt RNA excisions and ascribes the dominant rate-limiting step to the hybrid unwinding (Fig. 3l).

## Discussion 

In this work, we investigate the molecular mechanism of S. cerevisiae RNase H1 degrading RNA–DNA hybrids at the single-molecule level.

One of the interesting findings is that RNase H1, initially known as an endonuclease, also possesses intrinsic exonuclease activity. RNase H1 continuously eliminates RNA within the hybrid in the 3′-to-5′ direction, which can be initiated internally or from the 3′ end of the RNA (Fig. 6). Interestingly, this distinctive characteristic sets scRNase H1 apart from its E. coli counterpart, RNase HI, which relies on a 5’ end DNA overhang for the 5’-to-3’ exonuclease activity[38] . Moreover, E. coli RNase HI differs from scRNase H1 in the binding preference for RNA ends with DNA overhangs and yet decreased affinity for blunt ends or internal regions of RNA–DNA hybrids[38] . This discrepancy is likely due to the marked structural differences between E. coli RNase HI, lacking a hybrid binding domain (HBD), and scRNase H1, which features two HBDs[17][,][18] . A few nucleases have been acknowledged to possess both exonuclease and endonuclease activities, and the transitions between these activities are functional in DNA metabolism[39][–][41] . For instance, following the introduction of an internal breakage of dsDNA as endonucleases, FEN1 and Mre11 are found to consecutively carry out exonucleolytic cleavage as exonucleases, resulting in a gap or an overhang in the DNA for the following DNA repair[40][,][41] . Therefore, it is plausible that RNase H1 makes full use of its dual enzymatic activities in effectively degrading

Taking advantage of the high tempo-spatial resolution of the smFRET method, we also unveiled the dynamics and kinetics of RNA–DNA hybrid cleavage by RNase H1. As an exonuclease, RNase H1 was found to iterate the duplex unwinding and exonucleolytic degradation during processive hybrid cleavage (Fig. 3). A 6-bp duplex is unwound within each catalytic cycle, and instead of mononucleotides, the frayed ssRNA is excised three ribonucleotides at a time for RNase H1 (Fig. 6). This iteration resembles the behaviour of the Rrp44 and EXD2 exonucleases, which also unwind duplexes before nucleotide excision[27][,][29] .

This cyclic coupling between duplex unwinding and nucleotide excision could be explained by a spring-loaded mechanism wherein the chemical energy released from the hydrolysis of the nucleic acids chain is converted into elastic energy for unwinding several base pairs in bursts and translocating directionally[29] . The overall reaction rate of RNase H1 is mainly governed by the hybrid unwinding, coupled with a relatively fast ssRNA excision (Fig. 3). A simple model hasbeen previously proposed to explain the processivity of RNase H1: a single hybrid binding event mediated by the HBD domain of RNase H1 permits the engagement of its hydrolyzing domain HC with a few adjacent sites on an RNA–DNA hybrid for cleavage[42] . Our findings enrich this model in that RNase H1 is also equipped with a motor-like property that can direct its directional movement along the hybrid after the adjacent RNA cleavage. This property fundamentally enables RNase H1’s processive hybrid cleavage. It is noteworthy that scRNase H1 distinguishes from other RNase H1 nucleases in that it contains two HBD domains[18][,][43] . Whether and if yes, how the two HBD domains contribute to the directional translocation along the hybrid warrants further exploration. 

Our work also has important implications for understanding the coordination of RNase H1 and RPA in processing the intracellular RNA–DNA hybrids and R-loops. Based on our findings, two mechanisms underlining the stimulation of RNase H1’s nuclease activity by RPA have been put forth: first, RPA enhances the rate and processivity of the intrinsic 3′-to-5′ exonucleolytic cleavage of RNase H1; second, RPA stimulates RNase H1’s exoribonuclease activity in the 5′-to-3′ direction (Fig. 6).

Similar bidirectional stimulation effects of RPA have also been reported on the BLM helicase-mediated dsDNA unwinding[44] . Given that hybrid unwinding is a prerequisite for RNase H1 to cleave ssRNA, it 

is conceivable that both stimulation pathways for RNase H1 are mainly achieved by RPA destabilizing the hybrid duplex. This notion is further supported by the results from the smFRET assays with the forked substrate and the optical tweezers assays using higher forces (Fig. 5, Supplementary Fig. 23). The direct interactions of RNase H1 with RPA may also help with its exonuclease activity. RPA has been previously demonstrated to promote the association of RNase H1 to RNA–DNA hybrids[22] . This promotion may help recruit RNase H1 to the hybrid fork and maintain its longstanding association for processive hybrid cleavage (Fig. 4). 

The stimulation of RNase H1’s bidirectional hybrid cleavage by RPA provides a clue for understanding the degradation of a long stretch of an RNA–DNA hybrid or an R-loop in DNA repair and recombination[9][–][11] . According to the literature, under cellular stress, both RNA–DNA hybrids and R-loops can be quite long and sometimes reach up to 10 kbp in length, while the RNase H1 concentration is estimated to be in a few nM range in cells[11][,][14] . One can imagine that an endonuclease introducing distributive cleavage along such a long substrate would not efficiently remove the RNA. Complete RNA elimination requires multiple rounds of association and dissociation of the endonuclease with the substrate. However, the internal nicking and the bidirectional hybrid cleavage by RNase H1 ensure the best use of the nuclease and allow for the removal of RNA within a long stretch of a hybrid or an R-loop in a timely fashion (Fig. 6).

Overall, this work unveiled the dynamics of RNase H1 cleaving hybrid and the regulatory effect of RPA on hybrid cleavage, which help identify the precise cellular functions of RNase H1 and deepen our understanding of the maintenance of genome stability.

## – Preparation of RNA DNA hybrid templates 

The RNA–DNA hybrid templates used in the optical tweezer assays were prepared through the following steps (Supplementary Fig. 1a, b, Supplementary Table 2)[50] . The templates typically consist of a twosided biotinylated ssDNA and a paired ssRNA. A dsDNA segment was PCR-amplified from the lambda DNA (Thermo). Using this dsDNA segment and a biotin- or digoxigenin-labelled primer, a second asymmetric PCR produced the ssDNA. The resulting dsDNA and ssDNA were separated by agarose gel electrophoresis and purified using GeneJET Gel Extraction Kit (Thermo). The 3′ end biotin labelling of the ssDNA was performed using biotin-dATP (Invitrogen) and terminal transferase (NEB). A dsDNA containing a T7 promoter (T7 DNA) at the 5′ end was PCR-amplified from lambda DNA, from which the ssRNA was transcribed. UTP-Cy3 was used in the transcription for the fluorescence labelling of the template.

The final RNA–DNA hybrid templates 

were produced by annealing the two single-stranded nucleic acids in the TE buffer. 

For substrates of smFRET experiments and gel-based bulk cleavage assays, DNA and RNA oligonucleotides with or without labels used to construct the templates were purchased from Sangon Biotech and GenScript, respectively. The RDH substrates for the smFRET experiments and gel-based bulk cleavage assays were produced by mixing fluorophore-labelled DNA or RNA with complementary RNA or DNA at a molar ratio of 1:1.5 in the annealing buffer containing 10 mM Tris–HCl (pH 8.0), 50 mM KCl and 1 mM EDTA. The mixtures were incubated at 95 °C for 3 min and then slowly cooled to room temperature within 3 h. Annealed templates were stored at −80 °C before use. ## Single-molecule optical tweezer assay and data analysis 

Single-molecule optical tweezer assays were performed at 25 °C on an instrument combining three-colour confocal fluorescence microscopy with dual optical traps (LUMICKS C-trap, Netherland)[51][,][52] . In the assay, an RNA–DNA hybrid molecule was initially captured between two streptavidin-coated polystyrene beads (1.76 μm in diameter, Spherotech) or between one streptavidin-coated polystyrene bead and one anti-digoxigenin-coated bead (2.01 μm in diameter, Spherotech). This hybrid tether was then transferred to channels as specified for each assay. Experiments on RNase H1, RNase H1-Cy3, and/or RPA-eGFP were – conducted in the reaction buffer containing 25 mM Tris HCl (pH 7.5), 50 mM KCl, 1 mM MgCl2, 0.05 mg/mL BSA, 1 mM DTT, 0.8% D-glucose, 1 mg/ml glucose oxidase, 0.4 mg/ml catalase, and 2 mM Trolox.

Imaging of RPA-eGFP utilized a 488-nm excitation laser, while imaging of – RNase H1-Cy3 and RNA(Cy3) DNA hybrid employed a 532-nm excitation laser. The confocal pixel size was set at 50 nm with a pixel dwell time of 1 ms. Custom software from LUMICKS was employed for singlemolecule data analysis. Pseudocolors were applied in Zen 3.2 software (Zeiss) for enhanced signal contrast visualization. For fluorescence signals, the total pixel intensities of the DNA–RNA hybrid or ssDNA region were summed up in each frame using Fiji. A linear fitting to the hybrid extension traces measured DNA extension rates in nm/s. The processivity in nm was calculated using fluorescence signals of RNase H1-Cy3 or RPA-eGFP. In this work, Li et al. study the RNA cleavage mechanism by RNase H1 from Saccharomyces cerevisiae. These proteins are particularly interesting as they degrade RNA solely when bound in RNA-DNA heteroduplexes. In addition to their biological relevance in maintaining genome stability, their specificity makes them highly interesting for applications in biotechnology and DNA-based nanotechnology. Therefore, understanding the molecular mechanisms involved in RNA cleavage by RNase H1 is a highly relevant topic.

Here, the authors employ state-of-art single-molecule optical tweezers and single-molecule FRET experiments, complemented by gel electrophoresis experiments, to probe the RNA cleavage dynamics of RNase H1. First, they find that RNase H1 possesses both endoribonuclease and processive exoribonuclease activity. Additionally, they demonstrate that the exoribonucleolytic activity is limited to the 3’-to-5’ direction, and is occurring in a duplex unwinding step followed by a nucleotide excision step. They show that the unwinding occurs in 6 nt steps and the excision results in 3 nt RNA fragments. Furthermore, they find that the presence of RPA facilitates the 3’-to-5’ degradation and enables the 5’-to-3’ exonuclease activity, by pre-separating the RNA-DNA heteroduplex.
